title: To amend the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands to make that Act applicable to hardrock minerals.
official_title: To amend the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands to make that Act applicable to hardrock minerals.
likelihoodReason: Sponsored by Rep. Fallon (R-TX) with 2 cosponsors; passed the House and was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. Expanding domestic hardrock-mineral leasing has bipartisan appeal on supply-chain grounds, though it still needs Senate floor time.
summary: Extends the federal leasing system for minerals on government-acquired lands to hardrock minerals such as base and precious metals, industrial minerals, and gemstones.
brief: Makes the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands apply to hardrock minerals.

top_lines.headline: Hardrock Minerals on Acquired Lands
subs: Hardrock minerals added to the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands
Covers base and precious metals, industrial minerals, and gemstones
Excludes coal, oil, gas, sulfur, sodium, potassium, and Materials Act minerals

sections.label: Section 1 — Application of Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands to Hardrock Minerals

items.main: Makes hardrock minerals leasable under the Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands (30 U.S.C. 351 et seq.).
items.detail: Restructures the definitions in Section 2 (30 U.S.C. 351) and adds a definition of 'hardrock mineral' covering minerals found in sedimentary or other rocks, base metals, precious metals, industrial minerals, and precious and semi-precious gemstones — but not coal, oil, oil shale, gas, sodium, potassium, sulfur, or materials under the Materials Act of 1947 (30 U.S.C. 601 et seq.). Section 3 (30 U.S.C. 352) is amended to add hardrock minerals to the minerals the Act covers.

gaps: The bill makes hardrock minerals leasable on acquired lands but does not set royalty rates or lease terms specific to them.
It applies only to lands acquired by the United States and does not change leasing on the broader public domain.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Fallon
featured_quotes.text: if critical minerals like lithium are essential to our military and to our national security, if that is the case, then why are we still relying on our number one global adversary to supply them? China is mining about 18 percent of all the lithium in the world. With the United States, that percentage is less than 1. As far as refining, China is about 67 percent, some estimates up to 80 percent, where the United States is at 2 percent. For years now, the United States has been overly reliant on the communists in Beijing.

modified: Mineral Leasing Act for Acquired Lands (30 U.S.C. 351, 352) now applies to hardrock minerals (base and precious metals, industrial minerals, and gemstones), excluding coal, oil, gas, sulfur, sodium, potassium, and Materials Act minerals
"Hardrock mineral" definition: clause (iv) changed from "industrial metals" to "industrial minerals"
removed: Short title section dropped — the "Mineral Extraction for Renewable Industry and Critical Applications Act of 2025" / "MERICA Act of 2025" citation is gone; the hardrock-minerals provision is now the bill's only operative section
